definition: A UI pattern library documents reusable approaches to recurring interaction problems, such as entering an address or reviewing information before submission. A pattern explains how components, content, and behavior work together in a particular kind of task.
contentMarkdown:
# Pattern Library

A UI pattern library documents reusable approaches to recurring interaction problems, such as entering an address or reviewing information before submission. A pattern explains how components, content, and behavior work together in a particular kind of task.

## What belongs in a UI pattern?

A useful pattern describes the problem, the context in which the approach works, its interaction flow, and the decisions a team must adapt.

It can include relevant components, example content, accessibility considerations, and known limitations. The goal is to help someone solve a recurring problem, not simply reproduce a screenshot.

Teams use “pattern library” differently. State whether a particular library includes interaction patterns, component examples, visual styles, or a combination.

## Pattern library vs. component library vs. design system

| Resource | Main question |
|---|---|
| Component library | Which reusable building block can I implement? |
| Pattern library | How can those pieces support this recurring task? |
| Design system | Which shared decisions, resources, and practices govern the experience? |

A button is a component. Reviewing a request before sending it is a pattern that can combine headings, summaries, change links, and a confirmation action.

A pattern can be implemented using different components while retaining its important interaction principles.

## Example: reviewing a booking change

Suppose several products need users to review a proposed booking change. The pattern identifies the original and proposed values, any relevant consequences, and a clear route to correct a detail.

It also specifies what happens after submission, including an uncertain or failed result. One product may present this in a page, another in a dialog, depending on the task and constraints.

The pattern should explain which decisions are shared and which depend on the product. It should not invent a universal approval rule for every booking workflow.

## How do you create and maintain a pattern library?

Start with a repeated need observed in real product work. Compare existing implementations and the evidence behind them. Document the common approach and the reasons for any differences.

GOV.UK's pattern collection illustrates guidance organized around tasks and information needs, alongside a separate component collection.

Assign an owner and link working examples. Check that the pattern still fits the components and product constraints it depends on. When teams repeatedly need exceptions, investigate the pattern's scope instead of adding a new near-duplicate for every screen.

## Related terms

- [Component Libraries](/glossary/component-libraries.html)
- [Component Architecture](/glossary/component-architecture.html)
- [Design System Documentation](/glossary/design-system-documentation.html)
- [Design System Governance](/glossary/design-system-governance.html)

name: AI-ready Design System
definition: An AI-ready design system makes its supported components, design decisions, and usage rules accessible to AI tools, with a way to check the resulting work. Here, AI-ready describes a preparation goal rather than a particular product or file format.
contentMarkdown:
# AI-ready Design System

An AI-ready design system makes its supported components, design decisions, and usage rules accessible to AI tools, with a way to check the resulting work. Here, AI-ready describes a preparation goal rather than a particular product or file format.

## What does an agent need from a design system?

An agent needs reliable implementation context, not simply a screenshot of the intended style.

| Need | Useful system material |
|---|---|
| Find an existing component | Catalog, package location, and import example |
| Use it correctly | Supported API, states, and working examples |
| Follow visual decisions | Token roles, themes, and explicit exceptions |
| Build a complete interaction | Pattern guidance, content rules, and accessibility expectations |
| Check the result | Relevant tests, review criteria, and a route for unresolved gaps |

Keep these references aligned with the actual component version. Exposing outdated guidance through a tool makes it easier to retrieve, not more accurate.

## Example: generating a filter panel

A task asks an agent to build filters for an operations table. The system provides the real select and date-range components, their supported properties, the filter behavior, and examples with long labels.

The acceptance criteria include clearing filters, preserving entered values after an error, and keyboard operation. If the available date component cannot represent the required range, the agent records that gap instead of inventing a property.

Review the panel in the table workflow, not only as an isolated visual.

## Which tools can provide the context?

[Figma Code Connect](/glossary/figma-code-connect.html) can connect design components to code references. [Storybook](/glossary/storybook.html) can expose component examples and, through configured AI features, structured component documentation.

An MCP integration is a delivery mechanism. It does not determine whether the underlying content is complete or whether the output meets product requirements.

Choose the smallest useful workflow first. A maintained component guide and examples may be enough to test the approach before adding more integration work.

## How is this different from a design harness?

AI readiness describes the condition of the system's context and verification support. A [design harness](/glossary/design-harness.html) is the task environment that assembles references, constraints, and checks for implementation.

Evaluate readiness with representative tasks. Inspect component selection, supported API use, behavior, and the amount of correction required. Do not infer success from a visually plausible generated screen.

## Related terms

- [Design Harness](/glossary/design-harness.html)
- [Design System Documentation](/glossary/design-system-documentation.html)
- [Figma MCP Server](/glossary/figma-mcp-server.html)
- [Evaluation Harness](/glossary/evaluation-harness-ai-evals.html)

- [shadcn/ui](/glossary/shadcn-ui.html)

## Sources

- [Code Connect introduction, Figma](https://developers.figma.com/docs/code-connect/)
- [Manifests, Storybook](https://storybook.js.org/docs/ai/manifests)

name: Alt Text
definition: Alt text is a short text alternative for an image, usually provided through the HTML `alt` attribute. It conveys the image’s purpose or information in context so people can understand or use the content without seeing the image.
sources: An alt Decision Tree, W3C WAI (https://www.w3.org/WAI/tutorials/images/decision-tree/)
contentMarkdown:
# Alt Text

Alt text is a short text alternative for an image, usually provided through the HTML `alt` attribute. It conveys the image’s purpose or information in context so people can understand or use the content without seeing the image.

## What should alt text say?

| Image purpose | Text alternative |
|---|---|
| **Informative** | Convey the detail the image adds to the page. Describe the information someone would miss if the image were unavailable. |
| **Decorative or fully repeated in nearby text** | Use an empty attribute, `alt=""`, for an HTML image that adds no information or action. Screen readers can skip it. |
| **The only content in a link or button** | Name the destination or action. An image that opens a booking should help name the link “View booking.” |
| **Complex, such as a chart or map** | Identify the image in the short alternative and provide its essential details in nearby text, a linked description, or a data table. Pick the format that preserves the information people need. |

## Example: Three images on a hotel page

An atmospheric lobby photo beside an overview may be decorative. A photo that documents the accessible entrance could use “Step-free entrance with automatic sliding doors” if that is what the photo shows and the detail is missing from the text. A thumbnail that is the only content of a link to the full gallery could use “View hotel photos.”

Write the alternative for the role the image plays on each page. If an image sits beside visible text within the same link and adds no useful information, use `alt=""` and let the text name the link. Keep the empty attribute in the HTML. If it is omitted, some screen readers may announce the file name. When reviewing the page, check what a screen reader announces and whether someone can still complete the task with the image unavailable.

## Related terms

- [Accessibility and WCAG](/glossary/accessibility-wcag.html)
- [Semantic HTML](/glossary/semantic-html.html)
- [Content Modeling](/glossary/content-modeling.html)

## Sources

name: Design Debt
definition: Design debt is the accumulated burden of unresolved design decisions and problems that make a product harder to use, change, or maintain. It can result from deliberate shortcuts, inconsistent implementations, or assumptions that were never revisited.
sources: The Custodial Era of UX: Cleaning Up After AI, NN/g (https://www.nngroup.com/articles/ai-ux-debt/)
contentMarkdown:
# Design Debt

Design debt is the accumulated burden of unresolved design decisions and problems that make a product harder to use, change, or maintain. It can result from deliberate shortcuts, inconsistent implementations, or assumptions that were never revisited.

## What counts as design debt?

Examples include inconsistent validation across similar forms, duplicate patterns with unclear ownership, or interaction rules that repeatedly cause confusion.

The debt metaphor is useful when an unresolved issue creates continuing cost or makes future changes more difficult. Not every unbuilt idea or visual preference belongs in a debt backlog.

A design can also become unsuitable as users, tasks, or constraints change. Record what is now failing rather than assuming the original decision was careless.

## Design debt vs. technical debt

Technical debt concerns implementation choices and their effect on future development. Design debt focuses on interaction, information, content, and shared design decisions.

They can overlap. A duplicated form pattern may create both confusing behavior for users and repeated maintenance work for engineers. Resolving one side does not automatically fix the other.

Martin Fowler's technical-debt discussion distinguishes deliberate and inadvertent choices. That distinction can also help teams discuss the context of a design shortcut without treating every issue as individual failure.

## Example: inconsistent validation

Suppose three quote forms validate phone numbers differently. Users receive conflicting instructions, support answers the same questions repeatedly, and each rule change requires separate work.

The team investigates the actual requirements. It agrees on shared behavior, updates the component and guidance, and migrates the affected forms.

The useful result is consistent, appropriate validation. Making every error message look identical without resolving the underlying rules would leave much of the problem in place.

## How do you prioritize design debt?

Record the affected task, evidence, recurring cost, scope, owner, and a concrete remedy. Consider user impact, frequency, dependencies, and effort.

Separate a verified problem from a hypothesis that needs research. Prefer solving a shared cause over repeatedly correcting its symptoms when the evidence supports that scope.

Check the result after remediation. Count fewer repeated defects or observe improved task performance using a consistent method. A shrinking issue list alone does not establish that the most consequential problems were resolved.

## Related terms

- [Design System Audit](/glossary/design-system-audit.html)
- [Design QA](/glossary/design-qa.html)
- [Design System Governance](/glossary/design-system-governance.html)
- [Component Architecture](/glossary/component-architecture.html)

## Sources

- [Technical Debt Quadrant, Martin Fowler](https://martinfowler.com/bliki/TechnicalDebtQuadrant.html)
- [The Custodial Era of UX: Cleaning Up After AI, NN/g](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/ai-ux-debt/)

name: Design QA
definition: Design QA is the review of an implemented interface against its intended design and experience requirements. It checks whether the working product presents information and behaves as expected across relevant states, content, devices, and input methods.
sources: How to test UIs with Storybook (https://storybook.js.org/docs/writing-tests)
contentMarkdown:
# Design QA

Design QA is the review of an implemented interface against its intended design and experience requirements. It checks whether the working product presents information and behaves as expected across relevant states, content, devices, and input methods.

## What does design QA cover?

A useful review considers the task, not only how closely a screenshot resembles a design file.

| Area | Example check |
|---|---|
| Information and content | Correct labels, values, hierarchy, and error instructions |
| Interaction | Validation, loading, cancellation, success, and failure |
| Responsive layout | Long content, narrow views, zoom, and overflow |
| Accessibility | Keyboard operation, focus, semantics, and perceivable feedback |
| Shared system use | Correct components, tokens, variants, and intentional exceptions |

Define the acceptance criteria before implementation where possible. Resolve unclear requirements rather than treating every difference as a defect.

## Example: reviewing a request form

Suppose the design shows a quote-request form and confirmation. In the working preview, the reviewer enters a long name, submits an invalid email address, and tests a delayed response.

The field labels remain visible, the error identifies the problem, entered values are retained, and the completion message reflects the actual result. The reviewer also checks keyboard access and the mobile layout.

If the button looks correct but submits the request twice, visual approval is insufficient. Record the behavior, reproduction steps, expected result, and affected environment.

## Design QA vs. software QA vs. design critique

Software QA covers broader product quality, including areas such as functional correctness and integration. Design QA contributes experience-specific criteria and review.

A [design critique](/glossary/design-critique.html) examines a design proposal and its reasoning. Design QA checks what was implemented. Either can reveal that the intended design itself needs revision.

Keep responsibility collaborative. A designer can identify a discrepancy without being the sole owner of every test or fix.

## Which checks can be automated?

[Visual regression testing](/glossary/visual-regression-testing.html) can flag appearance changes. Interaction and accessibility tooling can test configured cases. Storybook provides ways to build checks around component stories.

These methods need appropriate coverage and review. Automated accessibility tools cannot establish full accessibility on their own, and component tests do not exercise every product workflow.

Retest the specific issue after a fix and check the surrounding task when it may be affected. Record accepted exceptions so the same intentional decision is not repeatedly reported as a defect.

## Related terms

- [Visual Regression Testing](/glossary/visual-regression-testing.html)
- [Storybook](/glossary/storybook.html)
- [Web Accessibility Audit](/glossary/web-accessibility-audit.html)
- [Design-to-Code Workflow](/glossary/design-to-code-workflow.html)

## Sources

- [How to test UIs with Storybook](https://storybook.js.org/docs/writing-tests)
- [Evaluating Web Accessibility, W3C WAI](https://www.w3.org/WAI/test-evaluate/)
